question: The EU summit in Cyprus and the irresponsible and damaging interview which Prime Minister Donald Tusk gave to the Financial Times1 in this context confirm a worrying shift in the EU’s security thinking.

Increasing importance is being attached to an expanding catalogue of political concepts, such as European strategic autonomy or a European army, which undermine the role of NATO and could lead to the United States being gradually pushed out of Europe. At a time of unprecedented threats to our continent, this is extremely dangerous and short-sighted, especially from the perspective of the eastern flank countries.

I was therefore concerned to learn that the Commission had begun work on operationalising the mutual assistance clause (Article 42(7) TEU). Although the provision itself may constitute an important element of solidarity between Member States, it should not be used to redefine transatlantic relations or to diminish the role of the United States in Europe’s security system.

The cornerstone of this system is NATO and its key pillar is Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty. The EU’s mutual assistance clause will not replace the deterrence guarantees provided by the Alliance, in particular through the US military presence and capabilities. I would therefore like to ask: 1.

How does the Commission intend to ensure that the work on operationalising the EU’s mutual assistance clause and the implementation plan being drawn up are not exploited or interpreted as measures which weaken the role of NATO, undermine the significance of Article 5 of the Alliance or damage transatlantic relations?
Is this work being coordinated with the North Atlantic Alliance and key allies, including the United States?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.7.2026) In the current volatile geopolitical environment, strengthening the EU’s crisis preparedness has become essential. The discussions on Article 42(7) of the Treaty on European Union (TEU)1 are part of the EU’s broader reflection on the future of EU security and defence.

The Treaty is clear: the implementation of the mutual assistance clause is entirely the prerogative of EU Member States. Ongoing reflections focus on clarifying how Member States may invoke it, the necessary coordination and the possible support from EU institutions, if requested by the affected Member State. For the 23 Member States that are also NATO allies, NATO remains the cornerstone of collective defence.

Article 42(7) of the TEU itself explicitly recognises this reality, stating that it shall not prejudge the specific security and defence policies of certain Member States, including those linked to neutrality or NATO obligations.

Ongoing work will by no means replace the deterrence and defence guarantees provided by NATO, nor should it be interpreted as weakening its role or undermining the significance of the provisions of Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty2.

On the contrary, discussions on the implementation of Article 42(7) of the TEU are being conducted in coordination with NATO, with the aim of ensuring coherence, complementarity and mutual reinforcement between the two frameworks, including through clear and coherent strategic communication.
